User: Here's my situation for 2024 taxes. I'm single, live in San Diego CA. My employer Desert Sun Logistics paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $8,900 doing consulting for 4 clients, got $920 interest from Marcus savings account and $195 dividends from Fidelity. I work from home in a 165 sq ft office; rent is $2,100/month, total space 850 sq ft. I paid $4,800 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2019), gave $800 to Northwest Harvest (food bank) I have the receipt, and had $780 in work supplies. Wha

t's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
Assistant: Thanks — good details. Below is a practical, step‑by‑step summary of what’s deductible, how to treat the home office, whether to itemize, rough numbers from what you gave, and the forms/worksheets to use.

What’s taxable income (quick overview)
- W-2 wages: $84,900 (report on Form 1040)  
- Self‑employment (consulting): $8,900 — report on Schedule C (Form 1040).  
- Interest: $920 (1099‑INT) — report o

n Form 1040 (no Schedule B needed because total interest+dividends < $1,500).  
- Dividends: $195 (1099‑DIV) — report on Form 1040.

Self‑employment and business deductions
- Report consulting gross receipts ($8,900) and business expenses on Schedule C.
- Deductible business expenses you listed: supplies $780 — goes on Schedule C (Line for supplies/other expenses).
- Home office deduction (see below) — also on Schedule C (Line 30). That reduces self‑employment profit.
- You will owe self‑employment tax on n

et profit from Schedule C; compute on Schedule SE. You can deduct half of the self‑employment tax as an adjustment to income (Schedule 1).

Home office — key rules and your options
- Must be for the business (your consulting), used regularly, and exclusively for business (no mixed personal use).
- Your office (165 sq ft) / total home (850 sq ft) = 19.41% of home.
- Two methods:
  1) Simplified method: $5.00 × square footage (up to 300 sq ft). For 165 sq ft = $825 deduction. Simple, no Form 8829 required.

2) Regular (actual expenses) method: allocate actual home costs by percentage. You gave rent only: annual rent = $2,100 × 12 = $25,200. Rent × 19.41% = $4,888.24. If you have utilities, renters insurance, internet, etc., a portion of those can also be included which increases the deduction.
- Important: home office deduction applies only to your self‑employment income, not to W‑2 employment (since unreimbursed employee expenses are not deductible for federal returns after 2017).
- The home office deduction

cannot create an excessive loss for the business beyond what the business income allows (normal net loss/at‑risk or passive activity rules may limit losses in some cases). Practically: compute both methods (simplified vs actual) and pick the larger, but be aware the actual method requires Form 8829 and records.

Rough math using your numbers (illustrative)
- Business income: $8,900  
- Less supplies: $780 → $8,120 before home office  
- If you use actual home office allocation of rent only: −$4,888 → busine

ss net ≈ $3,232  
  - SE tax base = 92.35% × $3,232 ≈ $2,985 → SE tax ≈ $456 → half SE tax ≈ $228 (above‑the‑line deduction)
- If you use simplified method: business net = $8,120 − $825 = $7,295 → higher net; SE tax will be larger
- Decide which method yields the best overall tax outcome (often actual is larger here because rent allocation is big).

Student loan interest
- Qualified student loan interest deduction: up to $2,500 (above‑the‑line), subject to income (MAGI) phaseouts. Based on rough AGI from yo

ur numbers, you may be in or near the phaseout range — so the deduction could be reduced or eliminated. Check the IRS worksheet or your tax software using your final MAGI. You should receive Form 1098‑E from your loan servicer showing interest you paid.

Charitable contribution ($800)
- Deductible on Schedule A if you itemize. Because single filer standard deduction is typically much larger than $800, you will likely take the standard deduction unless you have other sizable deductible items (state & local t

axes, mortgage interest, other charitable gifts) that push your itemized total above the standard deduction.

Standard vs itemize — quick guidance
- Likely standard deduction will be better for federal taxes given only $800 charitable giving and no mortgage interest or big property tax payments reported. Student loan interest is an adjustment (doesn’t affect the itemize vs standard decision). To be sure, run a quick itemized-total calculation including:
  - Charitable $800
  - State income taxes (or sales/p

roperty taxes) you paid in 2024
  - Any other deductible items (medical >7.5% of AGI, mortgage interest, etc.)
